source: MAFF General Directorate of Agriculture, banana cultivation techniques manual, 2019, section IV introduction (general care)
text:
Roughly 5 months after planting, once flowering has begun on the mother plant, farmers should start thinning (desuckering) the shoots growing from the base of each clump, since a stool left to produce many suckers at once will compete for water and nutrients and reduce fruit size on the current bunch. Remove excess shoots on an ongoing basis, generally monthly, keeping only one or two well-placed follow-on suckers that will replace the mother plant after its bunch is harvested and the mother stem is cut down.

Cut away old, dry, or pest-damaged leaves regularly, since dead leaf material left hanging on the plant creates hiding places for insect pests and disease inoculum.

Once a bunch is set and filling out, prop the pseudostem with a forked bamboo pole (positioned to support the trunk without wounding it) to prevent the plant from toppling or the stem snapping under the weight of a heavy bunch, and tie or brace it further as needed as the bunch continues to grow. About 15 days after the last useful hand of fruit has formed, cut off the remaining male flower bud ("banana heart") below the fruit, since it no longer contributes to fruit development and its removal channels more energy into the developing bunch. Covering the developing bunch with a light plastic or cloth bag is also recommended, both to protect the fruit from birds and insects and to keep the skin clean and free of scarring for better market presentation.
